title: The Song of Moses
aka: song of Moses and the Lamb
lead: Two songs carry Moses' name: the victory song at the sea (Exodus 15) and the long warning poem he teaches Israel just before he dies (Deuteronomy 32), called Ha'azinu ("Listen") from its first word. The conquerors in Revelation sing "the song of Moses, the slave of God, and the song of the Lamb" (Revelation 15:3).

sections.b: The first song comes right after the crossing of the sea. Moses and the Israelites praise the LORD as a warrior who threw horse and rider into the sea, and the song looks ahead to the nations trembling and to God planting his people on his own mountain (Exodus 15:1–18). Miriam leads the women in its opening line with drums and dancing (Exodus 15:20–21). The second song comes at the end of Moses' life. God tells him to write it and teach it so that it will stand as a witness when Israel turns to other gods (Deuteronomy 31:19–22). It calls heaven and earth to listen, recalls God's care in the wilderness, accuses Israel of forgetting the Rock who gave it birth, threatens judgment, and ends with God taking vengeance on his enemies and making atonement for his land (Deuteronomy 32:1–43).

sections.h: How the two songs are related
sections.b: Both songs praise God as unmatched among the powers (Exodus 15:11; Deuteronomy 32:39) and both end with God settling his people in their land. But the first celebrates a rescue already won, while the second is a warning written for a failure still to come. Psalm 90, headed "a prayer of Moses," is the third poem tradition ties to him. Revelation joins the first song's setting, victors standing beside a sea, with words drawn from the Psalms and prophets, and calls it the song of Moses and of the Lamb (Revelation 15:2–4). Jewish worship uses both: Exodus 15 is sung every morning, and Deuteronomy 32 is the Torah portion Ha'azinu, read in the autumn between the New Year and the Feast of Booths.
